$comment: INVENTORY OF MCP SERVERS — copy this to inventory.json and edit it.
Each server is declared ONCE, here. The plugins (plugins/ folder) translate it
into each client's own format. You never edit a client's config by hand: you
edit here, then `manager apply` writes everywhere.
The 'system' entry below is the manager itself and should stay: it is how the
manager appears to your agents, so they can ask what is running and start what
is missing. Deleting it is allowed but you lose that.
Fields of a server:
transport       'stdio' (the client launches a process) | 'http' (the client calls a URL)
command / args  for stdio: the command and its arguments
url             for http: the MCP endpoint
why             WHY this server exists — the first thing an agent reads
notes           list of traps / preconditions (the KNOWLEDGE that travels with the config)
needs_service   id of a service from services.json to start before use (empty = none)
env             for stdio launched BY THE MANAGER: extra environment variables.
headers         for http called THROUGH THE MANAGER: extra HTTP headers.
Both are maps; both follow the secrets rule below. The manager expands
${NAME} from its own environment at the moment of use, and refuses the
launch/request with the variable's NAME when it is not set.
clients         list of plugin ids that receive this server.
ABSENT = ALL clients (a deliberate default: a client added
tomorrow inherits everything, and you restrict it afterwards if needed).
An empty list [] = NONE — it is a real value, not a way of writing 'all'.
An unknown id is refused at save/apply, not silently ignored.
SECRETS RULE: NEVER put a key or a token here. Reference an environment variable
name inside an env/headers value — "OPENAI_API_KEY": "${OPENAI_API_KEY}". The manager
expands ${NAME} from its own environment at the moment of use and refuses with the
variable's NAME when it is not set; the secret itself lands in no config file.

system.why: Manager of this machine's programs: see what is running, start what is missing.
notes: This is the concierge: services_list shows the REAL state and the WHY of each program.
It runs in the user's session (notification-area icon). If it is off, nothing can start it: it is the single bootstrap point.

example-stdio.why: Example of a server the client launches itself, over stdio.
notes: npx is used here because it is the most common; a direct binary works too.
On Windows some clients cannot launch 'npx' (a .cmd) without a shell — the opencode plugin handles that with command_prefix.

example-http.why: Example of a server already listening on a port, which the manager watches over.
notes: If this server needs a program running to exist, name it in needs_service and the manager will start it on the first call.
The tools stay VISIBLE even while the program is stopped, because the list is cached on disk.

example-restricted.why: Example of a server given to only SOME clients — the point of the matrix.
notes: Absent 'clients' means every client. A list means only those. An empty list means none.
Use it to save context: a small local model does not need twenty tools it will never call.
